questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Swedish firms that make repairing easier
How to fix a broken computer by yourself at home
Why Sweden has so much rubbish
The history of denim jeans
questions.why: They visit companies in Sweden making it easier to mend things instead of replacing them.

questions.q: Why does Sam say his day has been a nightmare?
options: He lost his job and his flat
He missed an important lecture
Several of his things broke
His bike was stolen from outside the office
questions.why: Sam says he ripped his jeans, his computer stopped working and his car wouldn't start.

questions.q: How successful was Fixi at the beginning?
options: It closed after only six months because of poor sales
It had only a few customers, mostly friends and family
It fixed six thousand bikes in its first year of business
It took more than six hundred orders in six months
questions.why: Rob says Fixi took more than six hundred orders in its first six months.

questions.q: What do Nudie Jeans offer their customers?
options: A cheaper price for students
Free repairs for life
A new pair every year
Jeans made from recycled bottles
questions.why: Rob says the jeans aren't cheap but they promise free repairs for life.

questions.q: Why did Fabia decide to buy Nudie Jeans?
options: She really liked the way they looked
They were cheaper than other jeans
Her brother told her to
She wanted to help the environment
questions.why: Fabia says she really liked the way they looked, so it was worth paying more.

questions.q: What do the innovators behind these companies say about their grandparents' time?
options: People bought new things more often
Nobody knew how to repair things
Repair shops were too expensive
Repairing broken things was normal
questions.why: Rob says they all say that in their grandparents' day it was normal to repair, fix and mend things.

questions.q: According to Jessika Richter, how will repairing become normal again?
options: Through new government laws that make repairs cheaper
As more people repair things and influence others
By making new products much more expensive to buy
By teaching repair skills to children in schools
questions.why: She says it's a peer effect: the more people repair, the more it will go mainstream.

questions.q: Why does Jessika Richter feel positive?
options: Because Swedes already buy very little
Because big companies have stopped making new products
Because repairing was once normal, so it's a return to the past
Because recycling is now easy
questions.why: She says it used to be mainstream, 'so that's what makes me positive too'.
